stories.summary: Kenya: AI Plot to Divide Opposition Ahead of 2027 Exposed 11 September 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Irene Mwangi Nairobi — An artificial intelligence-driven influence operation targeted former President Uhuru Kenyatta and former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua while promoting Energy Cabinet Secretary Opiyo Wandayi in a covert social media campaign ahead of Kenya's 2027 General Election, according to a threat intelligence report by global AI firm Anthropic. The operation, identified as GTG-54004, allegedly used Anthropic's Claude AI model to mass-produce political content designed to create the impression of spontaneous grassroots support and opposition to various political figures. According to the report, a single operator used AI to generate large volumes of social media posts, including narratives portraying the United Opposition as fractured and on the verge of collapse ahead of the 2027 elections. "The actor used Claude across several sessions to generate batches of exactly 50 tweets, explicitly instructing the model to make posts look like spontaneous grassroots commentary rather than a coordinated campaign," the report says. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The campaign allegedly targeted Gachagua and Kenyatta as part of efforts to portray divisions within the opposition movement. "Additionally, the network pushed stories claiming that Kenya's United Opposition coalition was breaking apart before the 2027 general election, directly targeting politicians Rigathi Gachagua and former president Uhuru Kenyatta," Anthropic said. The operation also pushed favourable messaging around Wandayi, particularly over his role in halting a scheduled electricity tariff increase.

stories.title: Sudan: Sudan's Civil Society Groups Reject El Burhan's Mooted Dialogue As 'Political Cover'
stories.summary: Sudan's Civil Society Groups Reject El Burhan's Mooted Dialogue As 'Political Cover' 10 September 2026 Dabanga (Port Sudan) Khartoum — Sudanese civil society coalitions and actors, the Darfur Women Platform, Sudan Civic Convergence Tracks, Sudan Peace Call, Tadamon, and Union's Front, have issued a categorical rejection of a proposed Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue sponsored by Gel Abdelfattah El Burhan and the country's military leadership, warning that a political process organised under the authority of one of the parties to the war cannot deliver either peace or legitimacy. In a joint statement issued today* ( to read the complete statement, scroll down to base of post ), the five Sudanese civil society coalitions and actors say the proposed "Preparatory Committee for the Sudanese-Sudanese Dialogue", announced in Khartoum at the invitation of the Sudanese Armed Forces leadership, lacks the neutrality, credibility, and inclusivity required for a genuine national process. Instead, they warn, the initiative risks becoming political cover for the consolidation of a de facto authority while the war continues and civilians pay the price. More than three years after the conflict began, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and devastating much of the country, the signatories argue that Sudan's crisis cannot be resolved through what they describe as a nominal dialogue conducted under military sponsorship. The coalition says any political process must reflect the aspirations of Sudanese people and support a lasting civilian democratic transition.

stories.title: Western Sahara: Spanish Lawmakers Back Citizenship for Sahrawis
stories.summary: Western Sahara: Spanish Lawmakers Back Citizenship for Sahrawis UN Photo/Evan Schneider The people of Dakhla City, Western Sahara 11 September 2026 Deutsche Welle (Bonn) By Shakeel Sobhan with AFP, Reuters Spanish lawmakers approved a bill that could give citizenship to tens of thousands of Sahrawis and their descendants, amid tense ties with Morocco. The legislation must now pass the senate. Spanish lawmakers on Thursday voted to grant citizenship to people born in Western Sahara under Spanish colonization — a region now that is now largely controlled by Morocco . The move could test Madrid's already delicate relations with Rabat, especially after the border crisis in Ceuta . The lower house approved the bill by: Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines In favor: 168 Against: 31 Abstentions: 145 The legislation would grant Spanish nationality to Sahrawis born before September 29, 1977, and allow their descendants to obtain citizenship through naturalization.

stories.title: Guinée: les nouvelles mesures de sécurité du maire de Kankan décriées
stories.summary: Guinée: les nouvelles mesures de sécurité du maire de Kankan décriées À Kankan en Guinée, c’est une décision controversée que viennent de prendre la mairie et la préfecture. stories.title: Cameroun: l’ambassade de France annule les contraintes financières pour les délivrances de visas étudiants
stories.summary: Cameroun: l’ambassade de France annule les contraintes financières pour les délivrances de visas étudiants Il y a trois mois, l’ambassade de France au Cameroun demandait aux personnes voulant étudier dans des écoles privées en France d'apporter la preuve du paiement intégral de la scolarité, ou une justification de la possession de la somme nécessaire. La mesure avait provoqué la colère et une manifestation devant l'ambassade. Mais dans un communiqué, l’ambassade a annulé sa décision, déjà contestée devant le tribunal administratif de Paris après la saisine de l’association Cap Études, un collectif de parents et d’étudiants du Cameroun. Publié le : 11/09/2026 - 04:30 Modifié le : 11/09/2026 - 10:16 2 min Temps de lecture Un étudiant camerounais avec une pancarte pour dénoncer le durcissement des conditions de délivrance de visas aux étudiants admis dans les universités privées en France, à Yaoundé le 14 juillet 2016. © RFI / Emmanuel Jules Ntap Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Avec notre correspondant à Yaoundé , Emmanuel Jules Ntap Le 4 septembre dans deux mémoires, puis le 7 septembre lors d'une audience des référés devant le tribunal administratif de Paris : le ministère de l’Europe et des Affaires étrangères et l’ambassade de France au Cameroun ont confirmé le retrait des mesures contestées. « Avec cette nouvelle décision, nous pouvons nous en tenir à la procédure classique, notamment pour certaines écoles, de payer un premier acompte de scolarité, ce qui implique donc moins de frais à mobiliser pour les familles, une décision cruciale surtout quand on connait les réalités de ces familles-là », explique Salomon Ondoua, coordonnateur de l’association Cap Études. De nombreuses fraudes dans les dossiers, selon l'ambassade de France Dans un communiqué, l’ambassade de France au Cameroun précise que chaque demande de visa fera toujours l’objet d’un examen rigoureux et une attention sera portée sur la « soutenabilité financière du projet de l’étudiant ».

stories.title: Madagascar: 13 centres d'arnaques en ligne chinois démantelés
stories.summary: Madagascar: 13 centres d'arnaques en ligne chinois démantelés Le ministère de la Justice américain a annoncé mercredi 9 septembre avoir participé au démantèlement de 13 centres d’arnaque en ligne établis à Madagascar et gérés par des ressortissants chinois. Ceux-ci pratiquaient le « scamming », une escroquerie destinée à tromper des internautes pour leur voler de l’argent ou leurs données personnelles. L’opération, menée conjointement avec les autorités malgaches et chinoises, a permis de remonter tout un réseau criminel transnational. 500 escrocs ont été arrêtés à travers le monde, dont une centaine sur la Grande Île, qui vont être transférés vers leur pays. Publié le : 11/09/2026 - 00:21 Modifié le : 11/09/2026 - 12:06 2 min Temps de lecture Treize centres d'arnaque en ligne ont été démantelés à Madagascar. © AP - Damian Dovarganes Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Avec notre correspondant à Antananarivo , Guilhem Fabry La présence d’Américains parmi les victimes de ce réseau criminel transnational a poussé les États-Unis à enquêter conjointement avec les autorités malgaches et chinoises. « Plusieurs agents du FBI et un représentant du ministère de la Justice américain sont venus à Madagascar en août », indique à RFI Tahindro Prospero Ranaivoson, le directeur de la coopération judiciaire internationale au ministère de la Justice. Selon ce magistrat, 160 ressortissants chinois ont été condamnés sur la Grande Île ces derniers mois dans cette affaire avant d’être incarcérés à la maison centrale d’Avaradrano.

stories.title: Africa: African Development Bank Group and African Forum of Deposit Funds Enter Into New Alliance to Mobilize More Long-Term Financing
stories.summary: African Development Bank Group and African Forum of Deposit Funds Enter Into New Alliance to Mobilize More Long-Term Financing 9 September 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) The African Development Bank Group and the members of the African Forum of Deposit Funds have agreed to strengthen their cooperation to mobilise more long-term financing for the continent's sustainable development. Through this strategic alliance, they aim to support productive investment, strengthen the continent's economic resilience and contribute to more inclusive growth. Recognising the importance of institutional cooperation, both parties intend to coordinate responses to geopolitical and economic uncertainties, climate-related disruptions, global shocks, market dependencies , and social economic divides. This structured and evolving cooperation framework respects each partners institutional diversity and complementary mandates. It strategically directs their joint efforts towards high-potential sectors aligned with their respective missions.

stories.title: Après la crise de Ceuta, le Maroc réagit et dit refuser d'être "un bouc émissaire"
stories.summary: Publicité Après la crise de Ceuta, le Maroc réagit et dit refuser d'être "un bouc émissaire" Afrique Plus d'un mois après l'afflux de migrants des 30 et 31 juillet à Ceuta, Rabat a répondu jeudi pour la première fois aux soupçons d'opération hybride qui pèsent sur le royaume chérifien. Mis en cause par plusieurs témoignages et un rapport de police espagnol, le Maroc a assuré qu'"aucune donnée, fait ou rapport n'établit une quelconque implication des autorités marocaines", rejetant la responsablité sur des "acteurs espagnols". Publié le : 10/09/2026 - 21:22 Modifié le : 10/09/2026 - 21:33 3 min Temps de lecture Partager Par : FRANCE 24 Des tentes sont installées le long de la plage à la suite des récentes traversées massives de migrants du Maroc vers Ceuta, en Espagne, le 2 septembre 2026. © Pedro Nunes, Reuters Le Maroc a affirmé jeudi 10 septembre qu'aucun élément ne permettait de l'impliquer dans l'afflux de migrants vers l'enclave de Ceuta fin juillet, et a dit refuser de servir de "bouc émissaire" à des "règlements de compte" en Espagne . Il s'agit de la première réaction publique officielle de Rabat depuis les événements des 30 et 31 juillet. Questions have been raised as to whether the late monarch indeed had a son as his family claims. Uganda 's traditional kingdom of Tooro has been plunged into a sucession crisis after the family of late monarch Oyo Nyimba rejected on Thursday other clan members' choice of successor. Although Uganda is a republic, it contains several ancient kingdoms whose leaders are still held in high regard as keepers of tradition and maintain significant social influence. stories.title: South Africa: Six South Africans Remain Unaccounted for After Nepal Flash Floods
stories.summary: South Africa: Six South Africans Remain Unaccounted for After Nepal Flash Floods 10 September 2026 SAnews.gov.za (Tshwane) Six South African nationals remain unaccounted for, following the devastating flash floods in Nepal, the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) confirmed on Thursday. DIRCO said it had, following a formal request from the Nepalese government, arranged with the South African Police Service (SAPS) for the collection and coordination of DNA profiles from biological relatives of the missing South Africans. The profiles were collected through the Victim Identification Centre under the SAPS Division: Detectives and Forensic Services and have been sent to police in Nepal and Interpol in Kathmandu. South African diplomatic missions in New Delhi, India, as well in Beijing, China, are also liaising with their respective host countries to coordinate the response to the disaster. "Regrettably, there is still no confirmation from the authorities in Nepal or China/Tibet regarding any of the six South African nationals. We will continue to monitor the situation closely and provide updates to the families as more information becomes available," DIRCO said.

stories.title: Royal family rift after popular TV news presenter chosen to succeed Ugandan king
stories.summary: Image source, UBC Image caption, UBC TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma has been selected as the new Tooro monarch By Wycliffe Muia Â and Â Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa Published 10 September 2026 A bitter succession dispute has erupted in one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms, days before the burial of its late king, who until his death had been the world's youngest reigning monarch. King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who ruled the Tooro Kingdom for more than three decades, was undergoing cancer treatment in the US when he died last month aged 34 . Royal clan elders have named popular TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56, as the next monarch, but this has been rejected by Oyo's close family. His sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said the late king had left a will written in 2022 naming his young son, whose identity has never been disclosed, as his successor. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Queen Best Kemigisa has appealed for the family to be allowed to bury her son in peace "My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday night of creating "confusion and turmoil" while the family was still grieving.

stories.title: Russia to open more cultural centres in Africa as it seeks to broaden influence
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Some "Russian Houses" already exist in Africa - including in key allies such as Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger By Makuochi Okafor BBC Africa Published 10 September 2026 Russia is expanding its network of cultural and educational centres in Africa as it seeks to strengthen ties beyond its military and security co-operation on the continent. The centres will promote the Russian language, education, science and culture, while supporting various projects, Russia's humanitarian agency says. Known as "Russian Houses", eight of 11 new centres are due to open in Africa, where 16 have already been set up over the years. Russia's state-controlled paramilitary force African Corps, which replaced the Wagner Group's mercenary operations, has become a key security partner for multiple military governments in the West Africa in the fight against jihadist insurgencies. In particular the juntas in Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso turned to the Russian mercenaries, now Africa Corps, as they sought to shrug off influence from their former colonial power France.

stories.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JTSL Unai Eizaguirre, an eel fisherman for 30 years, prepares gear with a colleague in the Basque Country Image: Nicole Ris/DW Advertisement In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades. The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species , which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels. "So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre, who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous." Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed. "The situation is so bad that we have to act on everything," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI.

stories.summary: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Police used tear gas to disperse hundreds of protesters who took to the streets on Monday over prolonged power cuts By Wycliffe Muia Â and Â Thomas Naadi Published 9 September 2026 The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa. His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours. "When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month. The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal. The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand. Frustration boiled over on Monday night, when protesters took to the streets in Banjul and surrounding areas, burning tyres and blocking roads over the prolonged power cuts.

Photograph: Indian Navy X/AFP/AFP/Getty Images Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia US-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia . Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August : one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey. Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has mainland Africa’s longest coastline.

stories.title: Morocco earthquake 3 years on: 'No one has remembered us'
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5Kwwu Some locals in the earthquake-hit town of Ighermane in Al Haouz, Morocco — like Mohamed Ait Belaid and his wife — are celebrating a new home after living in a tent Image: Zhor Baki/DW Advertisement On September 8, 2023, a devastating earthquake struck the Al Haouz region in Morocco , killing over 2,900 people, injuring more than 5,500 and causing widespread destruction. In the village of Ighermane in the High Atlas Mountains, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Marrakech, Mohamed Ait Belaid, 72, feels like things are actually going pretty well for him three years later. He had been living in a tent after the earthquake but now resides in a newly built house, even though it's smaller than the one destroyed in the earthquake. "I benefited from partial [state] support and received 80,000 dirhams [around €7,300] for rebuilding," he told DW. "I added about 100,000 [€9,110] dirhams from my own pocket. And thanks to God, I like my new house and I'm comfortable in it. I'm at peace because my wife, my children and I are all healthy and I haven't lost any of them." Around 40 kilometers away, in the town of Azgour, it's a different story.

stories.title: ‘This is what I have to do to survive’: the Sudan refugees forced into sex work
stories.summary: Illustration: Patrycja Podkościelny for The Guardian View image in fullscreen Illustration: Patrycja Podkościelny for The Guardian ‘This is what I have to do to survive’: the Sudan refugees forced into sex work They fled a brutal civil war to reach safety in Egypt, but now many Sudanese women and girls are falling prey to sexual exploitation S udanese women who fled to Egypt to escape the war in their country are facing increasing levels of sexual exploitation, with the Guardian told of single mothers forced to sell their bodies to survive and feed their children. Many of the women have not previously worked in Sudan , where conservative social norms dictate that men are usually responsible for financial support. Without established trades or professions, and with their husbands and other family members dead or missing, many female refugees are struggling to pay for food, medical care and rent. The Guardian spoke to 19 aid workers, refugees and medical professionals who say a lack of access to healthcare, education and, at times, food has made the situation for Sudanese women in Egypt increasingly desperate. Sudan’s civil war triggered the world’s worst displacement crisis, forcing more than 4.5 million people to flee to neighbouring Chad, South Sudan, Libya and Egypt.

stories.title: Nigerian academic on rags to riches: 'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
stories.summary: Image caption, David Etor's first break came after designing and building a kind of "solar oven" in Nigeria By James Diamond ,Â Bristol Â and Â John Darvall ,Â BBC Radio Bristol Published 7 September 2026 A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field. David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in the School of Electrical, Electronic and Mechanical Engineering at the University of Bristol. He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our dignity" in front of neighbours. "I didn't see a way out," he said. 'The poor called us poor' Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his memoir, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom. "It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said. "I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water. "[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food... "She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water. "She was trying to protect our dignity." stories.title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
stories.summary: Image caption, The Mercator projection is the map widely used across the globe but inaccurately depicts the sizes of countries and continents By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 5 September 2026 Updated 6 September 2026 The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents such as Africa. The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy with the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger. The UN adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own. There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks. Mercator map Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Mercator projection has been around since the 16th Century and was vital for navigating the oceans The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.

stories.title: Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The embrace of Russia by Niger, and other Sahel states, has been seen as a rejection of the post-colonial Western powers By Simi Jolaoso Africa correspondent Published 5 September 2026 When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia. Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport. Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger. Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny". "This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule." The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.

Composite: equal-earth.com, Getty Images UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland The United Nations has voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size. In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design. At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution.
